bibl.title: Long-lasting effects of subliminal affective priming from facial expressions

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: We conclude that behavioral biases induced by masked emotional expressions are not ephemeral, but rather can last at least 24 hours.

span.label: subliminal affective priming from facial expressions
span.quote: Is this subliminal affective priming merely a transient phenomenon manifested in fleeting perceptual changes, or are long-lasting effects also induced?

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: To address this question, we investigated memory for surprise faces 24 hours after they had been shown with 30-ms fearful, happy, or neutral faces.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Unconsciously processed happy primes are proposed to shift attention toward the global configuration of the following face, which improves encoding and hence next-day recognition.
span.quote: In line with this reasoning, we speculate that happy primes may have led to better encoding and subsequent memory by preferentially engaging an attention focus on the global configuration of facial features, consistent with findings that happy mood can increase the use of global features to classify visual figures ( Bridge et al., 2009 ; Frederickson, 2004 ; Gasper and Clore, 2002 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The prime's expression is proposed to alter encoding and/or later rehearsal of the target face, rather than the memory difference arising from the conscious affective judgment the participant made about that face.
span.quote: Therefore, we suggest that the observed differences in memory were due to subliminal priming that led to differential processing at encoding and/or subsequent rehearsal as a function of facial expression.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Affect elicited by a masked stimulus is assumed to be diffuse and therefore to spill over onto whatever stimulus follows it in time, producing assimilation of prime valence into the target judgment.
span.quote: Presumably, the affect from a subliminal stimulus is diffuse in the sense that it can spill over onto a temporally adjacent stimulus.

span.label: Prime awareness may have gone undetected, so the strictly-subliminal grouping is not certain.
span.quote: Of course, it remains possible that prime awareness was missed by the subjective reports (e.g., because of forgetting), or that prime awareness occurred despite chance-level discrimination abilities

span.label: The objective awareness check may have had too few trials per participant to estimate discrimination ability well.
span.quote: Of course, for any of the 43 participants the number of trials may have been suboptimal for assessing discrimination abilities.

span.label: The 24-hour gap before the subjective awareness questions may have affected the answers given.
span.quote: The 1-day delay may have influenced the nature of the answers provided, but these questions nonetheless provided indications that some participants were aware of primes on Day 1.

span.label: A single study cannot cover the range of effects that different facial expressions have on behaviour and cognition.
span.quote: A single investigation cannot address the great variety of influences that facial expressions of various emotions have on behavior and cognition.

span.label: an OSCILLOSCOPE was used to check that primes really were on screen for 30 ms and that the software log matched
span.note: eliminates: that the prime was actually visible - a subliminal effect claimed on a duration the software reported but the hardware never delivered
span.quote: We used an oscilloscope to verify that primes were presented for 30 ms and that the software log of prime durations was accurate.

span.label: each face cropped with an elliptical stencil that removes the hair
span.note: eliminates: that participants respond to hair or head outline rather than to the emotionally relevant facial features
span.quote: Each face was cropped using an elliptical stencil to exclude hair, which can distract participants from emotionally relevant facial features ( Tyler & Chen, 2006 ).

span.label: subliminal affective priming
span.quote: Although subliminal affective priming in these cases may be regarded as a transient phenomenon manifested only in fleeting perceptual changes, here we question the tacit assumption that such phenomena are short-lived. Might unconscious affective processing also have long-lasting effects

span.label: transient
span.quote: Although subliminal affective priming in these cases may be regarded as a transient phenomenon manifested only in fleeting perceptual changes, here we question the tacit assumption that such phenomena are short-lived. Might unconscious affective processing also have long-lasting effects

span.label: long-lasting
span.quote: Although subliminal affective priming in these cases may be regarded as a transient phenomenon manifested only in fleeting perceptual changes, here we question the tacit assumption that such phenomena are short-lived. Might unconscious affective processing also have long-lasting effects

span.label: surprise faces
span.quote: Subliminal priming in this experiment had consequences for both immediate affective evaluation of surprise faces and later memory for the same surprise faces

span.label: valence
span.quote: Emotionally ambiguous facial expressions, such as surprise, derive their affective valence primarily through context. For example, a face with a surprise expression can appear positive in the context of a surprise birthday party or negative in the context of a grisly murder in a horror film. This emotional ambiguity makes surprise expressions especially susceptible to modulations of affective judgment ( Kim, Somerville, Johnstone, Polis, Alexander, Shin, & Whalen, 2004 ), and thus suitable for use as targets in subliminal priming paradigms

span.label: recognition memory
span.quote: We also found that affective evaluation per se influenced subsequent recognition memory. We calculated mean affective ratings for each surprise face across trials for each participant

span.label: A TACIT ASSUMPTION NAMED AND TESTED - that subliminal affective priming is `a transient phenomenon manifested only in fleeting perceptual changes`. The paper does not dispute that the effect exists; it disputes how long it is entitled to last, and it says the short-lived reading was never argued for, only assumed. Second record this sitting whose target is a belief its field holds without evidence
span.quote: Although subliminal affective priming in these cases may be regarded as a transient phenomenon manifested only in fleeting perceptual changes, here we question the tacit assumption that such phenomena are short-lived. Might unconscious affective processing also have long-lasting effects

span.label: `long-lasting` OPERATIONALISED AS AN INTERVAL, not as a rhetorical claim: memory for the primed faces is tested 24 HOURS LATER, with the 30-ms primes absent at test and the target faces intermixed with new ones. The conclusion is stated as a floor - biases `are not ephemeral, but rather CAN LAST AT LEAST 24 HOURS` - which is the honest form for a study that measured one interval
span.quote: We conclude that behavioral biases induced by masked emotional expressions are not ephemeral, but rather can last at least 24 hours. Introduction The influence of affective information on behavior is notable

span.label: A TARGET CHOSEN FOR ITS AMBIGUITY, with the reasoning written out: surprise `derives its affective valence primarily through CONTEXT` - the same expression reads positive at a surprise birthday party and negative in a horror film. Because the target has no fixed value on the measured dimension, any value it takes can be attributed to the prime. The stimulus choice is doing the work a control usually does
span.quote: Emotionally ambiguous facial expressions, such as surprise, derive their affective valence primarily through context. For example, a face with a surprise expression can appear positive in the context of a surprise birthday party or negative in the context of a grisly murder in a horror film. This emotional ambiguity makes surprise expressions especially susceptible to modulations of affective judgment ( Kim, Somerville, Johnstone, Polis, Alexander, Shin, & Whalen, 2004 ), and thus suitable for use as targets in subliminal priming paradigms

span.label: the awareness split, and it runs OPPOSITE to Van-den-Bussche2013: participants `likely to have processed primes supraliminally DID NOT respond differentially as a function of expression`. The effect belongs to the unaware group and vanishes in the aware one - whereas Van den Bussche, holding signal strength constant, found conscious trials strongest. Two records, opposite orderings, and the designs differ in exactly the way that matters
span.quote: Participants likely to have processed primes supraliminally did not respond differentially as a function of expression. These results converge with findings showing memory advantages with happy expressions, though here the expressions were displayed on the face of a different person, perceived subliminally, and not present at test. We conclude that behavioral biases induced by masked emotional expressions are not ephemeral

span.label: replicates → Li, Zinbarg, Boehm, & Paller (2008)
span.quote: In particular, our findings replicate and extend the findings of Li and colleagues (2008) , though several design features differed between these two studies.

span.label: extends → Li, Zinbarg, Boehm, & Paller (2008)
span.quote: In particular, our findings replicate and extend the findings of Li and colleagues (2008) , though several design features differed between these two studies.

span.label: contradicts → Charles, Mather, & Carstensen (2003)
span.quote: Our results differ from previous findings of better recognition memory among young adults for images of scenes depicting negative compared to positive affect ( Charles, Mather, & Carstensen, 2003 ).

span.label: long-lasting —contrasted-with→ transient
span.note: differs in: HOW LONG THE EFFECT IS ENTITLED TO OUTLIVE ITS PRIME - the transient reading limits it to fleeting perceptual changes; this paper shows a bias surviving 24 hours with the prime absent at test. The whole dispute is a duration · strength of the relation: 0.95 — THE PAPER'S ARGUMENT IN ONE EDGE, and the fifth time this sitting that a priming effect's status turns on its time course rather than its size - see Q-749.
span.quote: Although subliminal affective priming in these cases may be regarded as a transient phenomenon manifested only in fleeting perceptual changes, here we question the tacit assumption that such phenomena are short-lived. Might unconscious affective processing also have long-lasting effects

span.label: subliminal priming —causes→ affective evaluation
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.9 — The immediate half of the result. Grounded on the sentence that explains WHY the target can move at all - an expression whose valence comes from context is one a prime can supply context for.
span.quote: Subliminal priming in this experiment had consequences for both immediate affective evaluation of surprise faces and later memory for the same surprise faces

span.label: subliminal priming —causes→ memory
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE LONG-LASTING HALF, and the span deliberately carries the awareness split with it: the same sentence pair reports the effect AND that it did not appear in participants likely to have seen the primes. Quoting the result without that qualifier would overstate it.
span.quote: Subliminal priming in this experiment had consequences for both immediate affective evaluation of surprise faces and later memory for the same surprise faces

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Happy face primes led to more positive ratings than fearful face primes in the SS group [ t (14) = 2.58, p < .05], but not in the NSS group [ t (27) = 0.65, n.s. ].

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: There were no main effects of group [SS vs. NSS, F (1, 41) = 0.30, n.s. ], or prime expression [ F (2, 82) = 2.62, p = .07], nor was there an interaction between group and prime expression [ F (2, 82) = 1.01, n.s. ].

span.label: chi-squared
span.quote: Performance data on emotional-expression discrimination were subjected to χ 2 analyses.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: Magnitude of affective priming was not associated with the degree of objective discrimination ability for participants within either the SS group [ r = -0.40, p = .13] or the NSS group [ r = -0.11, n.s. ].

span.label: regression
span.quote: This same question was also approached with a regression analysis, in which we computed the slope for the linear correlation between mean affective rating and memory score for each participant

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: The mean valence ratings were 3.36 ( SD = 0.46) for surprise faces, 1.69 ( SD = 0.29) for fearful faces, 5.53 ( SD = 0.07) for happy faces, and 3.40 ( SD = 0.10) for neutral faces.

span.label: median split
span.quote: We then segregated these ratings for faces rated more negatively and those rated more positively, collapsing across data from all three prime conditions, with a median split made separately for each participant.

span.label: p-value
span.quote: Above-chance levels of expression discrimination were indicated by significant χ 2 ( p < .05) for 23 participants.

span.label: Surprise faces preceded by masked happy primes were rated more positively than those preceded by fearful primes, but only among participants classified as strictly subliminal.
span.quote: Happy face primes led to more positive ratings than fearful face primes in the SS group [ t (14) = 2.58, p < .05], but not in the NSS group [ t (27) = 0.65, n.s. ].

span.label: A day later, recognition of the same surprise faces was better for those that had been happy-primed than for fearful- or neutral-primed faces, with no fearful-versus-neutral difference.
span.quote: Mean hit rate was significantly higher for happy-primed surprise faces than for fearful-primed surprise faces [ t (14) = 2.95, p < .05], and for neutral-primed surprise faces [ t (14) = 2.28, p < .05], but did not differ between fearful-primed and neutral-primed surprise faces [ t (14) = 1.28, n.s. ].

span.label: Independently of priming, faces a participant had rated more negatively on Day 1 were better recognised on Day 2.
span.quote: Surprise faces rated more negatively were remembered better than surprise faces rated more positively.

span.label: The awareness grouping moderated the memory effect: prime expression changed recognition in the strictly subliminal group but not in the not-strictly-subliminal group.
span.quote: Furthermore, the finding that memory results varied with prime status (fearful versus happy) in the SS group but not in the NSS group was confirmed by a significant interaction between prime status and group [ F (1, 41) = 4.52, p < 0.05].

span.label: Affective priming was reliable only in the first half of the priming phase, weakening across blocks.
span.quote: The magnitude of affective priming, defined as the mean rating difference between surprise faces primed by happy faces and those primed by fearful faces, was high in the first three blocks [ M = 0.24, SD = 0.31, t (14) = 2.99, p < .01], whereas affective priming in the second three blocks was non significant [ M = 0.11, SD = 0.32, t (14) = 1.31, n.s. ].

span.label: How strongly a participant was primed was unrelated to how well that participant could objectively discriminate the prime expressions.
span.quote: Magnitude of affective priming was not associated with the degree of objective discrimination ability for participants within either the SS group [ r = -0.40, p = .13] or the NSS group [ r = -0.11, n.s. ].

span.label: The authors conclude that subliminal affective priming is not a transient perceptual effect but persists for at least a day.
span.quote: We conclude that behavioral biases induced by masked emotional expressions are not ephemeral, but rather can last at least 24 hours.

span.label: Strictly-Subliminal (SS) group
span.quote: The remaining 15 participants comprised the Strictly-Subliminal (SS) group.

span.label: Not-Strictly Subliminal (NSS) group
span.quote: Members of the Not-Strictly Subliminal (NSS) group, failing to satisfy at least one criterion, were more likely to have been conscious of primes; members of the Strictly-Subliminal (SS) group, satisfying both criteria, were more likely to have processed primes only subliminally.

span.label: magnitude of affective priming
span.quote: The magnitude of affective priming, defined as the mean rating difference between surprise faces primed by happy faces and those primed by fearful faces, was high in the first three blocks [ M = 0.24, SD = 0.31, t (14) = 2.99, p < .01], whereas affective priming in the second three blocks was non significant [ M = 0.11, SD = 0.32, t (14) = 1.31, n.s. ].

span.label: memory score
span.quote: A higher memory score thus reflects stronger memory.

span.label: emotional expression of the masked prime face (fearful, happy, neutral)
span.term: emotional expression of the masked prime face (fearful, happy, neutral)
span.quote: Subliminal primes portrayed either a fearful, happy, or neutral expression.

span.label: prime duration and backward-masking timing (30-ms prime, 300-ms mask)
span.term: prime duration and backward-masking timing (30-ms prime, 300-ms mask)
span.quote: Each trial began with the central presentation of a fixation cross for 500 ms followed by an affective prime for 30 ms, immediately backward-masked by a surprise face for 300 ms ( Figure 1 ).

span.label: affective valence rating of the surprise face (6-point scale)
span.term: affective valence rating of the surprise face (6-point scale)
span.quote: Participants were instructed to judge the valence of each surprise face upon its offset using a 6-point bipolar scale ranging from 1 to 6

span.label: next-day recognition confidence for the surprise faces (4-point scale)
span.term: next-day recognition confidence for the surprise faces (4-point scale)
span.quote: Participants made recognition confidence judgments on a keypad using a 4-point bipolar scale ranging from 1 to 4

span.label: prime-awareness group (Strictly-Subliminal vs Not-Strictly-Subliminal)
span.quote: Furthermore, the finding that memory results varied with prime status (fearful versus happy) in the SS group but not in the NSS group was confirmed by a significant interaction between prime status and group [ F (1, 41) = 4.52, p < 0.05].

span.label: counterbalanced assignment of surprise-face sets to prime categories
span.term: counterbalanced assignment of surprise-face sets to prime categories
span.quote: Surprise faces used in the priming phase were divided into three groups of 16 faces for counterbalancing with the three categories of primes.

span.label: normed valence of the stimulus faces
span.term: normed valence of the stimulus faces
span.quote: The mean valence ratings were 3.36 ( SD = 0.46) for surprise faces, 1.69 ( SD = 0.29) for fearful faces, 5.53 ( SD = 0.07) for happy faces, and 3.40 ( SD = 0.10) for neutral faces.

span.label: Forty-three — number of participants tested
span.quote: Forty-three undergraduate students at Northwestern University gave informed consent to participate for course credit.

span.label: 15 of the 43 — size of the strictly subliminal subgroup, the only group showing both key effects
span.quote: The SS group was composed of 15 of the 43 participants tested, and it was only the SS group that demonstrated both key effects.

span.label: 30 ms — duration of the affective prime face before backward masking by the surprise face
span.quote: Each trial began with the central presentation of a fixation cross for 500 ms followed by an affective prime for 30 ms, immediately backward-masked by a surprise face for 300 ms ( Figure 1 ).

span.label: 21-27 hrs (mean = 23.9 hrs) — delay between the priming session and the surprise memory test
span.quote: The second session occurred 21-27 hrs after Day 1 (mean = 23.9 hrs).

span.label: 2.64, 2.87, and 2.70 — mean confidence-weighted memory scores in the strictly subliminal group for fearful-, happy- and neutral-primed faces
span.quote: Mean memory scores in the SS group were 2.64, 2.87, and 2.70 for fearful, happy, and neutral conditions, respectively.

span.label: M = 0.24, SD = 0.31, t (14) = 2.99, p < .01 — size of the happy-minus-fearful rating difference over the first three blocks
span.quote: The magnitude of affective priming, defined as the mean rating difference between surprise faces primed by happy faces and those primed by fearful faces, was high in the first three blocks [ M = 0.24, SD = 0.31, t (14) = 2.99, p < .01], whereas affective priming in the second three blocks was non significant [ M = 0.11, SD = 0.32, t (14) = 1.31, n.s. ].

span.label: M = -0.22, SD = 0.30, t (42) = 4.88, p < .01 — mean per-participant regression slope relating affective rating to memory score, negative meaning better memory for more negatively rated faces
span.quote: Collapsing across data from all three priming conditions and both groups, the mean slope was negative and significantly different from zero [ M = -0.22, SD = 0.30, t (42) = 4.88, p < .01], demonstrating better memory for more negatively rated surprise faces.

span.label: 23 participants — number showing above-chance objective discrimination of the prime expressions
span.quote: Above-chance levels of expression discrimination were indicated by significant χ 2 ( p < .05) for 23 participants.
